title: France thrash Norway with three special goals by Dembele. Are they going to win the World Cup?
author: Jordan Campbell
content:
Ousmane Dembele scored a stunning first-half hat-trick as France cruised into the World Cup knockout stage as winners of Group I.

Norway made 10 changes to the starting XI that beat Senegal in their previous game, including resting their star striker Erling Haaland. The game had been billed as a battle between Haaland and Kylian Mbappe, but it was Dembele who stole the show with his three goals, before Desire Doue added a late goal to make it 4-1.

The 2022 finalists France, who were led by Guy Stephan at the Gillette Stadium because Didier Deschamps was back home mourning the death of his mother, were in control from the start, going 2-0 up in 20 minutes.

Norway hit back immediately after France’s second goal, though, scoring from the restart through Thelo Aasgaard. But in the 32nd minute, Dembele completed his hat-trick with a wicked finish into the far corner.

The win means that France will almost certainly face Sweden in New York on June 30, before a possible last-16 clash with Germany in Philadelphia on July 4. Norway, meanwhile, will play Ivory Coast in Dallas on June 30, and if they win that, then either Brazil or Japan in New York on July 5.

In the other match in Group I, Senegal secured a resounding 5-0 win against Iraq to give them a chance of advancing as one of the eight best third-placed teams.

James Horncastle, Mark Carey and Jordan Campbell analyse the key talking points…

If there is a symbol, other than Luis Enrique, of the change of mentality at Paris Saint-Germain, it is Ousmane Dembele. The photo of him staring down Yann Sommer with the intention of pressing the Inter goalkeeper in the 2025 Champions League final was indicative of a complete shift in his approach to the game. Dembele’s preparedness to chase down opponents and make PSG a team by leading from the front was rewarded not only with a first Champions League title. He retained it in Budapest in May as the reigning Ballon d’Or holder.

Since Enrique began using him as Kylian Mbappe’s replacement at centre-forward, Dembele has shown a new, determined side to himself. He scored nearly as many goals under Enrique at PSG as he did at Rennes, Dortmund and PSG combined. But he has rarely delivered for his national team. Dembele’s goal against Iraq in Philadelphia earlier in the group was his first in 20 appearances in major tournaments.

His overall return, going into Friday’s game against Norway, was unimpressive: eight goals and six assists in 61 caps for Les Bleus. The French media demanded more. Bixente Lizarazu, the 1998 World Cup winner, wrote of the need to “save private Dembele” in his L’Equipe column. Dembele must have read it with his morning café au lait and croissant.

The best version of Dembouz showed up at Foxboro. He offered a reminder of how difficult he is to read for goalkeepers and defenders. You never know if he is going to shoot with his left or his right. To him, it makes no difference.

And to think it took him almost four years to score his first three goals for France…Here, he completed a 32-minute first half off a combined xG of just 0.13 for all three shots. It was the second-earliest hat-trick in World Cup history after pub-quiz answer Erich Probst for Austria against Czechoslovakia in 1954.

As if Mbappe and the in-form Michael Olise weren’t already enough for opponents to reckon with, Dembele translating his club form to performances like this for his country only further underlines France’s status as favourites to reach a third final in a row.

James Horncastle

Dembele’s first-half hat-trick was as good a treble as you could ever wish to see. According to analysis by Opta, it also had the second-lowest expected goals rating of any treble scored at World Cups between 1966 and the present day.

A quick explanation: expected goals — commonly known as xG — is a metric that measures the probability a specific shot will result in a goal.

Today, Dembele’s treble came from an xG of just 0.19. To contextualise that, it made him one of just two players in the last 60 years to score a World Cup hat-trick from an xG rating of less than 0.6.

It’s esteemed company. At number five on that list is Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, whose 1982 hat-trick for West Germany against Chile came from an xG of 0.98.

In fourth place, Cristiano Ronaldo’s three against Spain in 2018 (0.91xG); that was the one that ended with the knuckled free-kick in stoppage time to make it 3-3.

Ahead of Ronaldo: the great Real Madrid and Spain midfielder Michel. He scored all the goals in a 3-1 win over South Korea at Italia 90 and, until this evening, that might have been the prettiest hat-trick in World Cup history. One gorgeous back-post volley. One free kick that found the top-corner from 30 yards. One slaloming run past three players.

But brilliantly taken as each of those goals were, they still added up to a comparatively decadent xG of 0.64, which Dembele’s 0.19xG comfortably relegated to third position all time.

He smashed home his first goal with his right foot in a crowded penalty area…

Then whipped his second into the far corner from outside the penalty area…

And after showing some fabulous footwork inside the box, Dembele made it three with another delicate left-footed finish into the far corner — again through a busy penalty area.

First on that Opta list? A player most will never have heard of. In 1982, Hungary’s Laszlo Kiss scored the fastest hat-trick in World Cup history, scoring three times in seven minutes 42 seconds in a 10-1 win over El Salvador — and from an xG of just 0.17. Dembele is now in second place on both lists; Kiss is also the only player to score a faster hat-trick.

And Kiss also holds one other record: he was the first and remains the only substitute to score three goals in a World Cup match, having only come on the 56th minute.

And for any English fans asking, Geoff Hurst scored his hat-trick in 1966 from an xG of 1.1.

Seb Stafford-Bloor

The Norway coach Stale Solbakken hinted that he would rotate his starting XI against France, with qualification to the round of 32 already secured. Few would have expected the changes to be quite as wholesale, as he swapped 10 players, including Haaland.

USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino made nine changes for Thursday’s defeat to Turkey, but the difference is that they had already secured top spot. Norway’s meeting against France was a straight shootout to decide the group winner and runner-up.

Their entire knockout route would be set depending on this, so to put out a second-string team came as a surprise. The only player to keep their place was Fredrik Aursnes — and even that was as a makeshift right-back due to injuries.

Solbakken’s decision likely came down to not attaching as much value to first spot as there usually would be. There is logic to it.

The winner plays Sweden and could then go on to face Germany in the last-16. The quarter-final tees up the potential to meet the Netherlands or Morocco.

In comparison, the runner-up faces Ivory Coast and then the winner of Brazil vs Japan. A quarter-final in that bracket offers up Mexico or England as the most likely opponents.

Is there much difference in the difficulty level of both paths? Solbakken clearly decided not to, especially with several of his players suffering cramps in the first two games due to the humidity.

But it was a bold decision to drop Haaland. The Manchester City striker is wired to want to play every minute — and that desire will have been strengthened by virtue of this being his first World Cup and already putting himself in contention for the golden boot with four goals in his first two games.

“We will need to be rested for the round of 32, both mentally and physically,” said Solbakken. “It could be that we need to play another 30 minutes of play and penalties. We have been here for five-six weeks in a hotel. It is a pressure cooker. Travelling, different hotels, MD-1 (press conferences the day before matches). So many elements that are different.

“We can’t be a nation that doesn’t understand what is required, as we have never been there (in the last 32). We cannot be too greedy. We have to be smart rather than greedy.”

The man charged with filling Haaland’s sizeable shoes, Crystal Palace centre-forward Jorgen Strand Larsen, had a difficult day. In most other generations, he would be the main striker at Norway, but he finds himself behind Haaland and Alexander Sorloth in the pecking order. This was only his 29th cap (just his 11th start) and he failed to add to his tally of six, missing a 50th-minute penalty.

Norway will hope that Solbakke’s decision not to attack this game at full strength will age well as the tournament unfolds.

Jordan Campbell

France’s struggles against Senegal in the first half of their opening game seem like a long time ago now.

Ever since Deschamps got Michael Olise and Dembele to swap positions, with the Bayern Munich winger moving to the No 10 role and the PSG No 9 switching to the right, France have gone to another level. They have a higher ceiling than anyone in the competition.

Granted, it was to be expected that they would sweep aside Iraq in Philadelphia. Norway heavily rotated in Boston, too, with Solbakken leaving Haaland and Martin Odegaard on the bench. But France’s best players are delivering. Mbappe, Doue and Dembele have all scored at the World Cup. So has Bradley Barcola. It is, perhaps, only a matter of time before Rayan Cherki joins them.

It is hard to find a weakness. Manu Kone has forced his way into the team after an excellent season at Roma, covering for Aurelien Tchouameni against Iraq and Adrien Rabiot today. Theo Hernandez was, perhaps, a little clumsy on the penalty he gave away. But his former AC Milan team-mate, Mike Maignan, bailed him out with a trademark stop.

France are on the same side of the draw as Germany, the Netherlands, Morocco, Spain, the United States and, possibly, Portugal. It will be a gauntlet to the final. But this team is capable of beating anyone.

James Horncastle

Much has been made of teams remaining tactically switched on after the much-maligned hydration breaks, but do not forget the old football adage: you are never more vulnerable than when you have just scored a goal.

France took that mantra to the extreme. Just seconds after Dembele put them two goals up, Norway hit back immediately from their kick-off. Like, immediately.

Just 79 seconds separated the two goals hitting the back of the net as Norway quickly worked the ball to Aasgaard, who played a simple pass to Andreas Schjelderup on the left flank — with the 22-year-old able to drive into the attacking third unchallenged.

Schjelderup’s return pass then found Rangers midfielder, Aasgaard, who provided a delicious drop of the shoulder that nearly sent Dayot Upamecano to a different zip code — before reversing his shot to the near post beyond a helpless, flat-footed Maignan.

Perhaps there was something pre-determined in Aasgaard scoring against the French. Born in Liverpool to a Norwegian father and a French mother in 2002, his middle name is Gerard, which feels too coincidental not to be linked with the Liverpool manager, Gerard Houllier, a Frenchman who was heavily involved with the France national team across his career.

Aasgaard calmly jogged back to the halfway line as French players looked blankly at each other. It was emblematic of the breathless opening quarter to the game, which was, ironically, halted shortly after for the cursory hydration break.
